Allama Prabhu
------------------------------------------
Allama Prabhu (12th cent. A. D.) is perhaps the most important leader of the Vīraśaiva (Śaivism of Karnataka) Movement along with बसवेश्वर. Born in Baḷḷigāvi (in the Shimoga dt. of Karna-taka) of the pious parents Nirahaṅkāra and Sujñāni, he showed extraordinary spiritual wisdom and maturity even as a child. According to one biographer हरिहर, he was married in his youth to one Kāmalatā, but renounced the world when she died at a young age. Another incident mentioned is his ‘conquest of Māyā,’ Māyā being a princess who fell in love with him. He successfully resisted her advances and continued his onward spiritual journey. It is perhaps this experience that is at the root of his vacana (lyrical prose composition) ‘māyā is not in woman, but in the eye that beholds her.’ His intense desire to get enlightenment took him to a highly competent गुरु (spiritual teacher) Animiṣayya sitting in a guhā (cave). It was by his grace that he was filled with शिव-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and bliss. Hence he has used the pen-name ‘Guheśvara’ in his compositions.
He is said to have enlightened गोरख्नाथ् (another famous medieval saint) and many śivaśaraṇas (Vīraśaiva saints) like Basava, Siddharāma, Muktāyakka, अक्क महादेवी, Goggayya and others.
His वचनस् are a class by themselves and have successfully expressed deep spiritual experiences through wonderful similes.
See also AKKA MAHĀDEVĪ, LIṄGĀYATA MOVEMENT and VĪRAŚAIVISM.

Alakṣmī
(‘goddess of misfortune’)
------------------------------------------
The created universe, having been projected out of God and sustained by Him, is naturally identified with Him. Hence evil is as much God as good is. It is another aspect, a reverse aspect as it were. This is a bold assertion made by हिन्दुइस्म्.
If लक्ष्मी is the goddess of wealth beauty and splendour, अलक्ष्मी, her opposite number, is misfortune personified. According to mythological accounts she was also born during समुद्रमथन (‘churning of the ocean’). Since she appeared earlier than लक्ष्मी, she is also called ‘Jyeṣṭhā’ (the elder one). A sage Dussaha (‘the unbearable’) by name, married her. According to another version it was the sage कपिल. अधर्म (unrighteousness) was their offspring.
Alakṣmī is usually shown as an old hag riding a donkey. She has a broom in her hand. A crow adorns her banner. Her image finds a place in some temples. When propitiated, she can dispel evil and grant prosperity.
She is sometimes identified with लक्ष्मी herself.
Being a part and parcel of this च्रेअतिओन् and hence of our life, misfortune is no less divinely ordained than fortune. It is perhaps to teach this great fact of life that even misfortune is deified.

alātaśānti
(‘stilling the firebrand’)
------------------------------------------
When an alāta or a firebrand is moved quickly in circles or in any other way, it creates the इल्लुसिओन् of circles or lines of fire. When the movement is stopped, the illusions also disappear. They were never produced by the firebrand in motion and hence never dissolve back into it when at rest.
This is a typical example used by the Buddhist school known as Vijñānavāda and successfully adopted by the famous Advaitin गौडपाद (500 A. D.). According to the Vijñānavādins, विज्ञान or मिन्द्, conjures up the external world which has no reality of its own. The मिन्द् with a series of succession of ideas is the only reality. The external world appears to be real even as the circle of fire appears to be.
Gauḍapāda uses the same analogy to a different purpose. It is चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् (or आत्मन्) that appears in manifold forms due to māyā. In reality these do not come out of it, nor do they return to it, for they do not exist (vide Māṇḍūkya Kārikā on Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, 4.47-52). The sole reality is the unchanging pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, śuddha-vijñaptimātra. This section of his Kārikās (the 4th) is named as Alātaśānti-prakaraṇa.
The analogy of alātacakra (firebrand moved in circles) is pre-Buddhist and is found in the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 4.24.

ālaya-vijñāna
(‘consciousness, the home of impression’)
------------------------------------------
Is the external world perceived through the senses real or unreal? If real, what is its nature? If unreal, what then, is the reality? These are the questions often raised and discussed by the Indian philosophical systems. The Vijñānavāda school of बुद्धिस्म् (also called the Yogācāra school) denies reality to the external world and considers it as ideas or states of the internal विज्ञान (consciousness or मिन्द्), which alone is real. This विज्ञान is the ālaya or abode of all impressions. Hence the name ‘ālaya-विज्ञान.’ It is the potential मिन्द् similar to the आत्मन् of other systems. However it is considered not as an unchanging substance, but as a stream of continuously changing states. Through proper culture it can gradually stop the arising of the undesirable mental states and develop into the ideal state of निर्वाण (emancipation).
See also VIJÑĀNAVĀDA and YOGĀCĀRA.

Alakanandā
------------------------------------------
Objects and scenes of natural beauty of this universe of phenomena have always fascinated the Hindu मिन्द्. Mountains, forests, rivers and seas have invariably provided the inspiration to build places of पिल्ग्रिमगे where human beings can contemplate the Divine and feel elevated.
Of the many rivers of India, गङ्गा (Ganges) stands unparallelled and supreme with regard to holiness and the number of places of पिल्ग्रिमगे associated with it. अलकनन्दा is one of its important tributaries which joins it at an early stage.
Taking its birth on the Indo-Tibetan border of Uttar Pradesh, it is joined by Nandākinī at Nandaprayāga, by Piṇḍar at Karṇaprayāga and Mandākinī at रुद्रप्रयाग. It joins भागीरथी at Devaprayāga. Here-after the rivers merged together go by the name गङ्गा. The famous विष्णु temple at बदरीनाथ is situated on the bank of अलकनन्दा.
See also GAṄGĀ.

ālasya
(‘lassitude’)
------------------------------------------
Ālasya or laziness is the worst enemy of man. When even material well-being is blocked by it, how can the lazy one hope for spiritual progress? That is why पतञ्जलि, the great teacher of योग, has listed it as an antarāya or obstacle in the path of योग (vide Yogasūtras 1.30). Since it is caused by an excess of तमस् (dark element among the guṇas), it is to be overcome by रजस् (activity) and सत्त्व (dynamic goodness).
Suśruta, the great teacher of Āyur-veda (Hindu system of medicine and surgery), considers आलस्य as a condition which inclines a man more towards pleasure and less towards work, though capable (vide सुश्रुत Saṁhitā, Śārīrasthāna, 4.51).

alaṅkāra
(‘embellishment’)
------------------------------------------
The word, derived from the root ‘kṛ’ (‘to do’) along with the prefix ‘alam’ (‘enough’, ‘sufficient’) means something that makes a thing more complete, a dress or an ornament. But it has acquired a more technical sense in the field of Sanskrit literature, viz., ‘figure of speech.’ The science that deals with this subject has been designated as ‘Alaṅkāraśāstra.’
See ALAṄKĀRA-ŚĀSTRA.

Alampur
------------------------------------------
Alampur is a village on the bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā River in the Mahaboobnagar district of Andhra Pradesh. The village is renowned for the Nava-ब्रह्मा temples (also known as स्वर्ग-ब्रह्मा temples) built in the 7th century A. D. Some of them are located within the same prākāra (outer wall). All are in the वेसर style, a combination of the नागर and द्राविड styles, though the former aspect is more prominent. They appear to be the prototypes of the temples developed fully at ऐहोऌए and बादामि now situated in the Karnataka State.
Alampur has sometimes been called Dakṣiṇa काशी.
See also AIHOḶE, BĀDĀMI, DRĀVIḌA, NĀGARA and VESARA.

Alaṅkāra-śāstra
(‘science of figure of speech’)
------------------------------------------
The सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे and Sanskrit literature have become an inalienable part of Hindu religion and culture. Even the earliest recorded specimens of Sanskrit literature have manifested the art of graceful speech. Several hymns of the Ṛgveda may be looked upon as genuine specimens of fine poetry. Various rhetorical devices now known as upamā (simile), rūpaka (metaphor) or atiśayokti (hyperbole) find an apt expression there in a natural way. The Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, though they are monumental works of wisdom and imagination, are also works exhibiting rare poetical skill.
Alaṅkāraśāstra as a regular, independent, subject might not have existed in more ancient times. The first systematization started perhaps with the Nāṭya-śāstra of भरत who might have existed some time during the period 200 B. C.—A.

. Though primarily a work on dramaturgy, the origins of systematization of poetics as a science can be discovered here. However, it is Bhāmaha and दण्डिन् (6th cent. A.D.), वामन and Udbhaṭa (8th cent. A. D.), Rudraṭa and Ānandavardhana (9th cent. A. D.), अभिनवगुप्त, Kṣemendra and Mammaṭa (11th cent. A. D.) that have enriched the literature on poetics through their prolific writings of superb quality.
The subject of अलङ्कार was viewed from different angles by different authors. This gave rise to eight sampradāyas or schools: rīti, गुण, अलङ्कार, vakrokti, रस, ध्वनि, अनुमान and aucitya.
Rīti is the way of writing. Though three rītis were originally recognized, they ultimately rose to six. The names given to them such as Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī or Māgadhī suggest that they were prevalent in particular regions. दण्डिन् and वामन were the forerunners of this school.
Guṇa or quality may concern either the शब्द (word) or the अर्थ (meaning). It is very similar to the Rīti school. Originally enumerated as three, it gradually rose to ten. However this school got merged into the अलङ्कार school. वामन was the chief exponent of this गुण school.
Alaṅkāra is literary embellishment. It may be of शब्द (word or sound) or अर्थ (sense). The alaṅkāras rose from 38 in the early period to 200 in later days. दण्डिन् and Bhāmaha were the main propagators of this school.
Vakrokti is equivocation. It is a mode of expression so that the listener conceives of a meaning different from that intended by the speaker or writer. Bhāmaha and Kuntaka (11th cent. A. D.) were the chief advocates of this school.
Rasa is mood or sentiment, a genera-lized resultant emotion in the spectator or reader. Nine rasas, often called ‘navarasas,’ have been advocated by the writers on prosody and dramatics. भरत was the earliest exponent of the रस school followed by Udbhaṭa and others.
Dhvani is suggestion. The theory of ध्वनि was introduced by आनन्द-vardhana.
Anumāna refers to a sentiment that has to be inferred and experienced. Śaṅkula (9th cent A. D.) was the founder of this school.
Aucitya means propriety. This school was propounded by Kṣemendra.
Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra, Bhāmaha’s Kāvyālaṅkāra, दण्डिन्’s Kāvyādarśa, Udbhaṭa’s Kāvyālaṅkāra-saṅgraha, Rudraṭa’s Kāvyālaṅkāra, Ānandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka and Mammaṭa’s Kāvya-prakāśa
are some of the standard works of अलङ्कार-शास्त्र.

Alakā
------------------------------------------
When रावण usurped लङ्का from कुबेर (the king of wealth), the latter retired to कैलास and propitiated Lord शिव through severe austerities. शिव got another beautiful city built by विश्वकर्म (the chief architect of the gods) and presented it to कुबेर. This is Alakāpurī or अलका.

alabdha-bhūmikatva
(‘non-attainment of yogic states’)
------------------------------------------
Yoga is defined as union of the indi-vidual सोउल् with the Supreme सोउल् through समाधि (perfect concentration, super-conscious experience). The path to this union is fraught with several obstacles. Of the nine obstacles technically known as ‘antarāyas’ mentioned by पतञ्जलि in his Yogasūtras (1.30) ‘alabdhabhūmikatva’ is the eighth.
In spite of the fact that the aspirant is correctly practising the various steps and disciplines of योग, he fails to attain any of the yogabhūmis or planes of psychic and spiritual experience mentioned in the text books of योग. This is called ‘alabdha-bhūmikatva.’ This is primarily due to the evil सṁस्कारस् or impressions carried over from past lives, which drain all the energy generated by yogic practices even as rat-holes in a field drain the water with which it is irrigated. With the help of the गुरु (spiritual preceptor) and by deep introspection he can discover his weaknesses and try to eliminate them by proper practices.
See also ANTARĀYAS.

Alakhnāmīs
(‘those who take the name of the Unseen’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic मोनस्तिचिस्म् as expounded in the धर्मशास्त्रस् was practically reserved for the ‘dvijas’ or the ‘twice-born,’ members of the first three castes. Spiritual aspiration, especially the desire for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, being common to all human beings, persons from outside these three caste groups too have evolved their own way of monastic life and monastic orders. One of the many such groups is the ‘Alakhnāmīs,’ also called ‘Alakhgīrs’ and ‘Alakhiyas.’ The word ‘alakh’ is a corrupted Hindi form of the Sanskrit word ‘alakṣya,’ the ‘unseen.’ So, the ‘Alakhnāmīs’ are those who take the name of the ‘Unseen,’ the Supreme ब्रह्मन्. They believe only in God without form.
This sect is said to have been started by one Lāl or Lālgīr, a saint of the camār (shoemaker) caste. It is not known when he lived.
Members of this sect are confined mostly to Bikanir in Rajasthan State. They wear a long blanket coat and a conical cap. While begging for alms or greeting one another they cry out ‘Alakh kaho,’ ‘Speak of the Unseen.’ They are gentle by nature and practise non-violence, catholicity and purity. They do not recognize चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् and disfavour visiting temples.
